content: Adult bronchiolitis was first described in 1899 by the University of Minnesota. In 1900, Dr. Lange, a German physician, provided a detailed description of its pathology and potential causes in two patients, establishing bronchiolitis as a distinct pathological entity. Adult bronchiolitis can be classified into six subtypes based on clinical syndromes and histological abnormalities: bronchiolitis obliterans, respiratory bronchiolitis, follicular bronchiolitis, proliferative bronchiolitis, airway-centered interstitial fibrosis, and diffuse panbronchiolitis. The pathogenesis of adult bronchiolitis involves inflammation and immunological responses that result in cellular injury and damage. This process can lead to respiratory compromise, which may become irreversible and fatal. Conditions such as asthma and primary immunodeficiencies are often associated with bronchiolitis. Gross pathology reveals destruction of bronchioles and airways, while microscopic findings include fibroblasts and lymphocytes. Common causes of bronchiolitis include inhalational injuries, viral infections, and drug-induced damage. Specific agents include mineral dusts, diacetyl, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and busulfan. Less common causes include organ transplantation, rheumatoid arthritis, and ulcerative colitis. The incidence of adult bronchiolitis is not well-documented. In the United States, it is estimated that 3 per 100,000 cases of community-acquired pneumonia have underlying bronchiolitis. The prevalence of adult-onset bronchiolitis remains unknown. RSV is the most common cause in adults, though many adults are asymptomatic or carriers, making prevalence difficult to determine. The mortality rate for bronchiolitis complicated by pneumonia in elderly care homes is approximately 3 per 100,000. The incidence increases with age, with a median age of diagnosis at 68 years. There is no racial predilection, but men are more commonly affected and have higher mortality rates. Diffuse panbronchiolitis is particularly common in Japan. Individuals of Hispanic, Native American, and Alaskan origins have a higher likelihood of hospitalization. Incidence, hospitalization, and mortality rates are similar in both developed and developing countries. Risk factors for developing adult bronchiolitis include smoking, cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, immunodeficiency, and immunosuppression. Without treatment, patients may develop symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and dyspnea. Common complications include chronic bronchitis, pneumonia, and death. Prognosis is generally excellent for viral bronchiolitis, with full recovery after treatment. However, occupational bronchiolitis is often irreversible and permanent. There is no single diagnostic test for adult bronchiolitis. The gold standard for diagnosis is clinical assessment. A history of insidious onset of cough, wheezing, and dyspnea, along with deteriorating pulmonary function, is suggestive of the condition. Common symptoms include cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath. Less common symptoms include hemoptysis, dehydration, and loss of appetite. Patients often appear lethargic. Physical examination findings may include bilateral basilar lung crackles, tachypnea, wheezing, and occasionally a low-grade fever. There are no specific laboratory findings associated with adult bronchiolitis. However, laboratory investigations such as complete blood count, white blood cell count, C-reactive protein, blood cultures, rapid viral antigen testing, arterial blood gases, pulse oximetry, urine analysis, sputum analysis, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and cultures may aid in diagnosis. Imaging studies, such as high-resolution chest CT scans, can be helpful. Findings on CT scans suggestive of bronchiolitis include mosaic or diffuse air trapping, bronchial wall thickening, linear opacities, centrilobular nodules, and bronchiectasis (dilated airways). X-rays may show nonspecific findings such as hyperinflation, lobar infiltrates, and atelectasis. Ultrasound may reveal aberrant lung patterns and subpleural consolidations. Oxygen-sensitive 3He-MRI is useful in detecting bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS) after organ transplantation, as normal grafts show higher oxygen distribution compared to those with BOS. Lung biopsy and histopathology can confirm the diagnosis and rule out other causes of dyspnea. Histopathological findings include abnormalities in the walls of membranous or respiratory bronchioles, tubular narrowing or obliteration of the lumen, concentric T-lymphocyte infiltration, smooth muscle hypertrophy in small airways, bronchiolectasia with mucus plugging, and fibrosis and scarring. The optimal medical therapy for adult bronchiolitis is unknown. Treatment primarily involves cessation of exposure to irritant agents. The disease is progressive and often leads to respiratory failure. Supportive therapy includes supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, cough suppressants, anti-reflux therapy, macrolides, immunosuppressants, and glucocorticoids. The use of bronchodilators and glucocorticoids is controversial and reserved for patients who show clinical improvement. Lung transplantation is not a first-line treatment and is typically reserved for patients with advanced, untreatable lung disease. Primary prevention measures include avoiding exposure to inhalants, smoking cessation, prevention of vaping, health awareness, and routine surveillance. Reducing exposure through the use of medical masks, respirators, robots, isolation of harmful processes, ventilation, limiting exposure hours, maintaining dust control systems, and using warning signs is also recommended. There are no established measures for secondary prevention of adult bronchiolitis.
